transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that reading for just 20 minutes a day can significantly reduce stress levels and improve overall mental health, according to researchers at the University of Sussex. The study measured stress levels in participants before and after different activities, and found that reading reduced stress by 68 percent—more than listening to music, going for a walk, or even drinking tea or coffee. Researchers say that reading requires concentration, which distracts the mind from worries and stressors, and it also relaxes the body by lowering heart rate and easing muscle tension. The study found that even just a few minutes of reading can have a calming effect, and it doesn't matter what you read—fiction, nonfiction, newspapers, or magazines all work. Researchers say that reading is a simple, cheap, and accessible way to improve mental health, and they recommend making it a regular part of daily life.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the University of Sussex study find about reading?
2. Why does reading reduce stress according to researchers?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of Vancouver in Canada has launched an innovative new program called "Play Streets," where certain residential streets are temporarily closed to car traffic on weekends and holidays so that children can play safely. The program is part of the city's efforts to create more public space and encourage physical activity, especially among children who may not have easy access to parks and playgrounds. During Play Streets events, streets are blocked off with barriers and signs, and kids can ride bikes, play games, and just be kids without the danger of cars. The city says that the program has been very popular so far, with more and more neighborhoods applying to host Play Streets events. Supporters say that Play Streets help build community, encourage children to be active, and make neighborhoods safer and more livable.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.

4. What is the purpose of the program?
5. What is one benefit of the program mentioned in the passage?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Researchers at Princeton University have found that taking notes by hand is more effective for learning and memory than taking notes on a laptop or other electronic device, according to a new study. The study found that students who took notes by hand remembered more information and understood concepts better than students who took notes on laptops. Researchers say that this is because taking notes by hand is slower and requires you to process information and summarize it in your own words, which helps with learning and memory. Laptop note-takers, on the other hand, tend to write down everything the professor says verbatim without really thinking about it. The study also found that laptop users are more easily distracted by email, social media, and other websites during class. The researchers suggest that students who want to improve their grades might want to put away their laptops and go back to pen and paper.

7. Why is handwriting notes better for learning according to researchers?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Mike): Hey Sarah, I heard you just got back from your trip to Japan. How was it?
Woman (Sarah): It was absolutely amazing! Japan is such a cool country—so different from anywhere I've ever been. I had the best time.
Man: I'm so jealous! I've always wanted to go to Japan. What did you do there?

Woman: Well, I spent a few days in Tokyo first. Tokyo is insane—so big, so busy, so much to see and do. I went to Shibuya Crossing, visited some temples, went shopping in Harajuku, ate tons of amazing food... I could have spent weeks just in Tokyo and not gotten bored.
Man: That sounds awesome. Did you go anywhere else besides Tokyo?

Woman: Yeah, I took the bullet train to Kyoto for a few days. Kyoto is completely different from Tokyo—way more traditional, with all these temples and gardens and geisha walking around. It was like stepping back in time. I also did a day trip to Nara to see the deer and the giant Buddha statue.
Man: Wow, that sounds incredible. What was the food like? I've heard Japanese food is amazing.

Woman: Oh my god, the food was the best part! Everything is so fresh and so delicious. I ate sushi, ramen, tempura, okonomiyaki, matcha everything... I gained like 5 pounds just from eating, but it was totally worth it. Even the convenience store food is good!
Man: Ha, that's what I've heard. What about the language barrier? Did you have trouble communicating?

Woman: A little bit, but it wasn't as bad as I expected. A lot of people in Tokyo speak at least a little English, especially in tourist areas. And there are pictures on most menus, so you can just point to what you want. I learned a few basic Japanese phrases before I went, which helped a lot. People are really friendly and patient, even if you don't speak the language well.
Man: That's good to know. What was your favorite part of the trip?

Woman: Hmm, that's hard to say. I loved Tokyo for the energy and the food, but Kyoto was so beautiful and peaceful. I think my favorite thing was just walking around the neighborhoods and exploring—finding little shops and cafes and temples that weren't in the guidebook. And the people were so nice and polite.
Man: It sounds like you had an amazing time. Would you go back?
Woman: Definitely! I already want to go back. There's so much more I want to see and do. Next time I want to go to Osaka and Hiroshima, and maybe spend some time in the countryside.
Man: I need to start planning my own trip. Do you have any tips for someone going for the first time?

Woman: Oh, lots of tips! First, get a Japan Rail Pass if you're going to be traveling between cities—it saves you so much money. Second, learn a few basic Japanese phrases—hello, thank you, excuse me. People really appreciate it. Third, don't be afraid to try new foods—even if you don't know what it is, it's probably delicious. And fourth, wear comfortable shoes because you'll be walking a lot.
Man: Great tips! Thanks, Sarah. You've made me even more excited to go.
Woman: No problem! You'll love it. Let me know if you need more help planning.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
8. What did Sarah think of Japan?
9. What did Sarah think of the food in Japan?
10. What was Sarah's favorite part of the trip?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Emma): Hey Liam, how's your university application going? Have you started working on your personal statement yet?
Man (Liam): Ugh, don't even get me started. I've been staring at a blank page for days. I have no idea what to write. How about you?
Woman: I've started, but it's really hard. How do you sum up your whole life and explain why you're the perfect candidate in just 4,000 characters? It's impossible.
Man: Exactly! And I don't even know if I'm applying for the right subject. I'm interested in so many things—history, English, politics... I don't know which one to choose.
Woman: Oh, I know what you mean. I went back and forth between psychology and sociology for ages. But I think I've finally decided on psychology.
Man: How did you decide?

Woman: Well, I thought about which subjects I enjoy the most in school, and which ones I could see myself studying for three years. And I also thought about what kind of job I might want after university. Psychology seems more versatile to me.
Man: That makes sense. I guess I should think about it more carefully. What are you writing about in your personal statement?

Woman: Well, I'm trying to show that I'm really interested in psychology beyond just what we learn in class. I'm writing about some books I've read, a documentary I watched, and some work experience I did at a counseling center over the summer.
Man: Oh, that's good. I don't really have any work experience related to what I want to study. Is that a problem?

Woman: Not necessarily. You can talk about other things—books you've read, projects you've done, hobbies, volunteer work, anything that shows you're interested in the subject and that you have relevant skills. The personal statement isn't just about what you've done—it's about who you are and why you're passionate about the subject.
Man: Yeah, I guess. But I still don't know where to start.

Woman: Start with why you're interested in the subject. What made you want to study it? Was there a particular moment or experience that sparked your interest? Start with that story, and then build from there.
Man: Hmm, that's a good idea. What about structure? How should I organize it?

Woman: I think the standard structure is: introduction about why you're interested in the subject, then evidence of your interest and relevant skills (reading, work experience, projects), then maybe something about your extracurricular activities and what they've taught you, and then a conclusion tying it all together.
Man: Okay, that makes sense. How long should it be?
Woman: The limit is 4,000 characters or 47 lines, whichever comes first. So you have to be concise. Don't waste space on clichés or things everyone says. Make it personal and specific to you.
Man: Right. Should I have other people read it and give feedback?

Woman: Definitely! Show it to your teachers, your parents, your friends... get as much feedback as you can. But don't let them rewrite it for you—it has to be your voice. And make sure you proofread it carefully for spelling and grammar mistakes.
Man: Yeah, that's important. Thanks, Emma. You've been really helpful. I feel a little less stuck now.
Woman: No problem! We can read each other's drafts and give feedback if you want. It's easier to see problems in someone else's writing than your own.
Man: That would be great! I'll send you mine once I have a rough draft.
Woman: Perfect. Good luck! And remember—everyone struggles with personal statements. You're not alone.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous and impressive structures in the world, but there are also many myths and misconceptions about it. While it's often called the "Great Wall," it's actually not a single, continuous wall—it's a series of walls, fortifications, and natural barriers built over many centuries by different Chinese dynasties.

One of the most common myths about the Great Wall is that it's visible from space with the naked eye. This is a widely repeated claim, but it's simply not true. Astronauts have confirmed that you can't see the Great Wall from the moon, and it's very difficult to see even from low Earth orbit without binoculars or a camera. The wall is only about 6 to 7 meters wide, which is too narrow to be visible from that distance. It's like trying to see a single hair from a kilometer away.

Another myth is that the Great Wall was built all at once by a single emperor. In reality, the wall was built and rebuilt over a period of more than 2,000 years, starting as early as the 7th century BC. Different dynasties built different sections, and many of the walls were not connected. The most famous sections that people visit today were mostly built during the Ming Dynasty, from the 14th to the 17th centuries.

People also often think that the Great Wall successfully kept invaders out of China. But in reality, the wall was only partially effective. While it did help defend against smaller raids, it wasn't able to stop major invasions. The Mongols, the Manchus, and other groups were able to get past the wall many times, either by finding weak points, bribing guards, or simply going around the ends of the wall. The wall was more of a psychological barrier and a symbol of Chinese power than an impenetrable military defense.

Despite these myths, the Great Wall is still an incredible feat of engineering and a testament to the hard work and ingenuity of the people who built it. It stretches for thousands of kilometers across mountains, deserts, and plains, and it's rightfully considered one of the wonders of the world. It's just important to separate fact from fiction when we talk about it.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect our emotions, behavior, and perceptions. While the idea that colors can influence our mood and behavior might sound like pseudoscience to some, there's actually real scientific research showing that colors can have measurable effects on how we think, feel, and act.

One of the most well-known effects of color is its impact on mood. Warm colors like red, orange, and yellow tend to be stimulating and energizing. Red is often associated with passion, excitement, and even danger—it can increase heart rate and blood pressure. Yellow is associated with happiness, optimism, and creativity. Orange is somewhere in between, combining the energy of red with the cheerfulness of yellow.

Cool colors like blue, green, and purple, on the other hand, tend to be calming and relaxing. Blue is often associated with trust, stability, and peace—it's one of the most popular colors for corporate logos because it conveys reliability. Green is associated with nature, growth, and health—it's often used in healthcare and environmental branding. Purple is associated with luxury, creativity, and spirituality.

But the effects of color are more complex than just "warm colors are exciting, cool colors are calming." Different shades and tones can have very different effects. A bright, saturated blue can be energizing, while a soft, muted blue can be calming. And context matters too—the same color can mean different things in different situations and cultures.

Culture is actually a very important factor in how we perceive color. While some color associations seem to be universal, others vary widely from culture to culture. For example, in Western cultures, white is associated with purity and weddings, but in many Eastern cultures, white is associated with death and mourning. Red is considered lucky and celebratory in China, but in many Western countries it's associated with danger and warning.

Color also affects our behavior in practical ways. Studies have shown that people are more likely to buy products in certain colors, that students perform differently in classrooms painted different colors, and that even sports teams wearing certain colors win more often. For example, some studies have found that teams wearing red uniforms win more often, possibly because red is associated with dominance and aggression.

Of course, color psychology isn't an exact science. The effects of color are often subtle, and they vary from person to person based on personal experience, culture, and individual preferences. But understanding how colors can influence us can be useful in many areas, from design and marketing to education and healthcare.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Urban agriculture—the practice of growing food in cities—has been growing in popularity around the world as people look for ways to eat healthier, reduce their environmental impact, and build stronger communities. From small backyard gardens to large community farms to rooftop gardens on office buildings, urban agriculture takes many forms and offers many benefits.

One of the most obvious benefits of urban agriculture is that it provides fresh, healthy food to city residents. In many cities, especially in low-income neighborhoods, it can be hard to find fresh fruits and vegetables—these areas are often called "food deserts." Community gardens and urban farms can help address this problem by growing fresh produce locally and making it available to people who live nearby.

Urban agriculture also has environmental benefits. Growing food locally reduces the distance food has to travel from farm to table, which cuts down on transportation emissions and packaging waste. Urban gardens can also help reduce the "heat island" effect in cities, where buildings and pavement absorb heat and make cities hotter than surrounding rural areas. Plants and trees provide shade and cool the air through transpiration. And urban gardens can help manage stormwater by absorbing rainwater that would otherwise run off into streets and sewers.

Another important benefit of urban agriculture is its social impact. Community gardens bring people together from different backgrounds and neighborhoods, creating opportunities for social connection and community building. They give people a chance to work together, share knowledge and skills, and take pride in their neighborhood. For children, gardens are a great way to learn about where food comes from and to develop healthy eating habits.

Urban agriculture can also have economic benefits. It can create jobs in farming, distribution, and food processing. It can help low-income families save money on groceries by growing their own food. And it can increase property values and revitalize blighted areas by turning empty lots into green spaces.

Of course, urban agriculture also faces challenges. Space is limited in cities, and good land can be hard to find and expensive. Soil quality can be poor, and there can be concerns about contamination from previous land use. Water access can also be a problem. And urban farmers often have to deal with pests, weather, and other challenges that all farmers face.

But despite these challenges, urban agriculture continues to grow and evolve. New technologies like hydroponics, vertical farming, and rooftop greenhouses are making it possible to grow more food in less space. And as more people recognize the benefits of growing food locally, urban agriculture is likely to become an increasingly important part of city life.

24. What is one environmental benefit of urban agriculture?
25. What is one challenge urban agriculture faces?
